main.title: Folklore
main.subtitle: Doolin, Ireland and an Otherworld to Cross
main.summary: Folklore is a 2007 action role-playing video game developed by Game Republic and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 3.

cards.heading: Ellen and Keats explore an Irish Otherworld
cards.text: Folklore is a 2007 action role-playing video game developed by Game Republic and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 3. Set in Ireland and the Celtic Otherworld of Irish mythology, the game follows two protagonists: a young woman named Ellen and a journalist named Keats, who work together to unravel the mysteries of the quaint village of Doolin by seeking the memories of the dead in the Netherworld.

cards.heading: Doolin as the hub between worlds
cards.text: Doolin serves as a hub between visits to the Netherworld. Ellen and Keats explore the village, talk to its inhabitants and follow quests that advance the mystery. Combat abilities are reserved for the other world, giving the village sections a quieter pace.

cards.heading: Capturing Folk with Sixaxis movements
cards.text: In the Netherworld, the gameplay shifts to action-adventure. Basic attack techniques are performed using folk; creatures and spirits that, when defeated, can be absorbed for use by the player. When a folk is near defeat, its spirit will glow red, allowing players to absorb it by locking onto it and performing shaking and pulling motions with the Sixaxis to reel in its energy. Only four folk can be assigned to the controller's four interface/action buttons at a time. Different kinds of folk are better suited for certain situations and techniques, such as melee combat, projectile attacks, or magic. The two playable characters also have different play styles. Ellen uses a variety of folk and specializes in defense, having the ability to cloak herself with folk powers, while Keats specializes in offense, using brute-force attacks and stronger folk, and has the ability to release built-up energy to become invincible and stronger for a duration.

cards.heading: The composers of Folklore
cards.text: The official Folklore soundtrack was released on 3 discs on June 27, 2007, by TEAM Entertainment. The music was composed by Kenji Kawai, Shinji Hosoe, Ayako Saso and Hiroto Saitoh. The song "Nephilim" by Japanese band Abingdon Boys School plays during the end credits.

main.title: The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass
main.summary: The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass is a 2007 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS handheld game console.

cards.heading: The Wind Waker continues on DS
cards.text: The Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass is a 2007 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS handheld game console. It is the fourteenth installment in The Legend of Zelda series and the direct sequel to the 2002 GameCube game The Wind Waker. Phantom Hourglass was released worldwide in 2007, with the exception of South Korea in April 2008. It was re-released for the Wii U via the Virtual Console service in the PAL region in November 2015, in North America in May 2016, and in Japan in August 2016.

cards.heading: Touch controls and the search for Tetra
cards.text: The game features 3D graphics with cel shading and an overhead camera perspective. It employs controls involving the console's touchscreen and microphone, and took advantage of the Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection for online play until the service was discontinued in 2014. The game's story is set some time after the events of The Wind Waker, focusing on series main character Link's journey to save his friend Tetra from the story's primary antagonist, Bellum, with the help of Linebeck and his ship, the S.S. Linebeck.

cards.heading: Reception and Spirit Tracks
cards.text: Phantom Hourglass received critical acclaim, with praise for its control scheme, world design, and graphics, while some criticized its online features, which were considered too simple. The game received several video game industry awards, including the Nintendo DS Game of the Year award from GameSpot, GameSpy, and IGN. Phantom Hourglass was the best-selling game in its first month in Japan, with 302,887 copies sold. In the United States, it was the fifth-best-selling game in the month it debuted, with 262,800 copies sold. 4.13 million copies of Phantom Hourglass were sold worldwide by March 2008. A sequel, Spirit Tracks, was released in December 2009.

main.title: Guitar Hero Encore: Rocks the 80s
main.subtitle: The last Harmonix encore
main.summary: A PlayStation 2 encore turns Guitar Hero II’s familiar stage into a celebration of eighties rock.

cards.heading: Thirty songs, one decade
cards.text: Released for PlayStation 2 in 2007, Guitar Hero Encore: Rocks the 80s concentrates its repertoire into thirty songs. New wave, hard rock and heavy metal share the same scrolling note highway, with familiar characters and venues dressed for the decade. Most recordings are covers, alongside a smaller group of artist recordings; even those require care when comparing editions, since the game’s I Wanna Rock uses a re-recording rather than the original album performance.

cards.heading: An encore rather than a reinvention
cards.text: The playing system closely follows Guitar Hero II: matching frets and strums keeps a performance alive, while Star Power can turn a carefully chosen phrase into a larger score. The attraction is a fresh repertoire rather than a new instrument or a full-band format. Its relatively small selection and limited mechanical changes divided reviewers. It was also Harmonix’s last Guitar Hero release before the studio moved on to Rock Band.

main.title: The World Ends with You
main.subtitle: Seven days in Shibuya
main.summary: The World Ends with You is Square Enix and Jupiter's Nintendo DS action role-playing game set in Tokyo's Shibuya district. Neku Sakuraba is forced into the Reapers' Game, where daily missions and uneasy partnerships determine his fate. The city's fashions, shops, food and mobile phones belong to its progression as much as to its appearance. Instead of sending a party into a distant fantasy landscape, the game makes a recognisable youth culture its world. Learning to engage with other people becomes part of Neku's journey through it.

cards.heading: Seven days in Shibuya
cards.text: The World Ends with You is Square Enix and Jupiter's Nintendo DS action role-playing game set in Tokyo's Shibuya district. Neku Sakuraba is forced into the Reapers' Game, where daily missions and uneasy partnerships determine his fate. The city's fashions, shops, food and mobile phones belong to its progression as much as to its appearance. Instead of sending a party into a distant fantasy landscape, the game makes a recognisable youth culture its world. Learning to engage with other people becomes part of Neku's journey through it.

cards.heading: A partnership across two screens
cards.text: Neku and his partner fight simultaneously on the DS displays, with the touchscreen carrying Neku's gestures and buttons controlling the character above. Equipped pins provide abilities triggered by actions such as slashing, tapping or other inputs. The arrangement asks the player to divide attention between two connected performances. A battle is therefore an exercise in cooperation even when played alone. Understanding one character's rhythm can make room to watch the other, turning the physical separation of the screens into an unusually direct expression of the partnership.

cards.heading: Wear the city into battle
cards.text: Clothing, food and pins give the people and businesses of Shibuya practical importance. Character development draws on things that might otherwise remain scenery in a role-playing game. The energetic soundtrack and angular character designs reinforce that connection to the district's streets. Missions organise exploration into individual days, providing a reason to return to familiar areas under different circumstances. The World Ends with You builds its identity from these connected choices: fighting, shopping and meeting people all help make the city more than a backdrop for the story.

main.title: Endless Ocean
main.subtitle: A dive with time to look
main.summary: Endless Ocean is Arika's Wii diving adventure set in the fictional Manaurai Sea. Guided by Katherine Sunday, the player explores underwater environments, identifies marine life and searches for sunken objects. Fish, dolphins and much larger animals give each destination another reason to linger. The structure makes observation the central activity of a diving game: learning what lives in a place and finding a route through its surroundings matter more than reaching a finish line. A boat provides a base from which another stretch of sea can be explored.

cards.heading: A dive with time to look
cards.text: Endless Ocean is Arika's Wii diving adventure set in the fictional Manaurai Sea. Guided by Katherine Sunday, the player explores underwater environments, identifies marine life and searches for sunken objects. Fish, dolphins and much larger animals give each destination another reason to linger. The structure makes observation the central activity of a diving game: learning what lives in a place and finding a route through its surroundings matter more than reaching a finish line. A boat provides a base from which another stretch of sea can be explored.

cards.heading: A sea made from different kinds of dive
cards.text: The Manaurai setting contains caves, wrecks, shallow areas and deeper trenches, bringing several forms of underwater exploration into one connected adventure. Discovering animals adds to the player's knowledge of the sea, and identified species can populate an aquarium. Dolphins and other cetaceans can become companions and learn behaviours. These activities encourage repeated visits with a different purpose each time. A route first followed to reach a location may later be worth revisiting because a particular animal, object or unfamiliar part of the environment has drawn attention.

cards.heading: A voice carries through the water
cards.text: Hayley Westenra contributes songs to the game, including Prayer and a performance of Pokarekare Ana. Their presence gives the quiet movement through the sea a distinct musical identity. Players can also provide MP3 files on an SD card for their own listening during a dive. The soundtrack becomes part of how an exploration is remembered: a slow passage beside a large animal or through an unfamiliar space acquires its own accompaniment. Endless Ocean leaves room for those encounters to become the memorable events of the journey.

main.title: Wild Arms XF
main.subtitle: A Western-flavoured world becomes a tactical map
main.summary: Wild Arms XF is Media.Vision's PSP tactical role-playing game, first released in Japan on 9 August 2007. It takes the Wild Arms setting into battles fought by a small squad across hexagonal maps. Characters develop through classes whose skills can later be combined, making preparation closely connected to the problem presented by the next encounter. The player has to consider how the group moves around an enemy as well as the strength of its weapons. Position becomes a shared resource, giving a carefully arranged formation opportunities that isolated fighters cannot create.

cards.heading: A Western-flavoured world becomes a tactical map
cards.text: Wild Arms XF is Media.Vision's PSP tactical role-playing game, first released in Japan on 9 August 2007. It takes the Wild Arms setting into battles fought by a small squad across hexagonal maps. Characters develop through classes whose skills can later be combined, making preparation closely connected to the problem presented by the next encounter. The player has to consider how the group moves around an enemy as well as the strength of its weapons. Position becomes a shared resource, giving a carefully arranged formation opportunities that isolated fighters cannot create.

cards.heading: Surround the target with a useful shape
cards.text: Formation Arts reward particular arrangements around an enemy, while Combination Arts allow several allies to connect their attacks. The same advantages can be used by the opposition, so an apparently strong position has to be checked for the response it permits. Class development adds another layer: permanently learned skills can be equipped outside their original class, allowing a character to combine roles. The player gradually builds a squad capable of solving different maps, then has to place those capabilities where they can work together. The hexagonal grid makes that arrangement visually distinct from a conventional square battlefield.

cards.heading: A portable branch with a flexible party
cards.text: Nobukazu Sato directed the game, with Akifumi Kaneko writing its story and a group of composers led by Masato Kouda supplying the score. Story characters can be joined by hired Drifters, giving more room to shape the squad. North American and European releases followed in 2008. The class system makes experimentation useful between battles, while the map rewards careful execution during them. Wild Arms XF therefore finds a tactical role for the series' setting, asking the player to express progress through the capabilities of a group rather than only the development of one central hero.

entries.event_semantics: The existing2007 North American release anchors the article; Finley's postmortem is retrospective production evidence. The manual describes the original Xbox360 version's fictional ADAM choice, not a statement about all remasters or every player's moral response.

cards.heading: Finding the city in one room
cards.text: BioShock's underwater city took shape through repeated revisions. Project lead Alyssa Finley recalls abandoning an early corridor-shooter prototype and returning to concept art. The team then built a single room, the Kashmir Restaurant, whose appearance became a reference for the rest of Rapture.

cards.heading: Rebuilding the player's first steps
cards.text: External playtests exposed another gap between the team's intentions and the player's experience. Finley describes people ignoring new powers, missing information and avoiding Big Daddies. Dialogue and backstory were overwhelming the lessons needed to play. The designers rebuilt the opening levels around a slower introduction to the systems, including combining weapons with plasmids. Rapture's density had to become understandable before it could become interesting. Her account also credits small teams from several disciplines with revising individual weapons, bringing animation, effects and sound into the same discussion.

cards.heading: ADAM and the Little Sisters
cards.text: Little Sisters carry ADAM, the substance used to buy additional powers, and Big Daddies protect them. After defeating a protector, the player can harvest a Little Sister or rescue her by removing the parasite. Rescue offers less immediate ADAM. Improving Jack's abilities is therefore tied to a decision about the children he encounters.

cards.heading: Entering Rapture
cards.text: Irrational Games released BioShock for Windows and Xbox 360 in North America on August 21, 2007. Jack explores Rapture, an Art Deco city built beneath the sea as a utopia and found after its collapse. Weapons, plasmid powers and security systems offer different approaches to its hostile inhabitants, while the damaged rooms reveal what happened to the city.

cards.heading: Designing the Art Deco city of Rapture
cards.text: Scott Sinclair served as Bioshock's art director. Once the Rapture setting was chosen, the art team began developing concepts of what the city would look like, inside and out. Art Deco worked well as a style for the environments because its large, simple shapes were easy to replicate with few polygons. The artists drew inspiration from a Gotham-style metropolis, with Hugh Ferriss's architectural illustrations and the Art Deco architecture of New York City providing inspiration for the look and massing of Rapture's skyline. Irrational also wanted to stay away from "tropical" art deco as seen in places like Miami Beach as it did not create the feeling they wanted. Hogarth De La Plante recalled that the team did not want to be too rigid in following a look, instead adapting the style according to their needs.

cards.heading: Weapons, EVE and Vita-Chambers
cards.text: Jack moves through Rapture with conventional weapons and plasmids that grant powers such as fire and electricity. The two systems answer different problems: a gun can be upgraded or loaded with another ammunition type, while a plasmid might melt a blocked passage or open an electrical lock. Plasmids consume EVE, recovered through supplies found in the city, and injuries require food or medical kits. Vita-Chambers return Jack to life nearby after defeat. Exploring therefore supports both the next fight and the means of reaching another part of Rapture.

cards.heading: Hacking security and researching enemies
cards.text: Rapture's systems can become tools rather than obstacles. Hacking a turret or security device redirects its usefulness, while plasmids can lure enemies into traps or turn them against one another. The hacking puzzle asks the player to connect a pipe route before time runs out, with failure risking injury or an alarm. A research camera rewards observing enemies with later combat advantages. Money and hacked vending machines replenish supplies, so a quieter investigation of the city can make a later confrontation easier.

main.title: Metroid Prime 3: Corruption
main.summary: Metroid Prime 3: Corruption is a 2007 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Wii.

cards.heading: The Prime series moves to Wii
cards.text: Metroid Prime 3: Corruption is a 2007 action-adventure game developed by Retro Studios and published by Nintendo for the Wii. The seventh main Metroid game, it was released in North America on August 27, 2007, followed by Europe on October 26, Australia on November 8,  and Japan on March 6, 2008.

cards.heading: Samus becomes infected
cards.text: Corruption is set six months after Metroid Prime 2: Echoes (2004). The player controls the bounty hunter Samus Aran, who becomes infected with Phazon by her doppelgänger, Dark Samus. Samus works to prevent the Phazon from spreading to other planets while being corrupted by the Phazon.

cards.heading: Aiming with the Wii Remote
cards.text: The player uses the Wii Nunchuk to move and the Wii Remote to jump, aim and fire. Corruption introduces features such as Hypermode, which allows Samus to use more powerful attacks, and the ability to command her gunship. The new control scheme took a year to develop and delayed the release several times. The game was first shown to the public at the E3 2005 trade show.

cards.heading: Reception and Metroid Prime: Trilogy
cards.text: Corruption received praise for its gameplay, graphics and music, though critics were divided on the controls. It sold more than one million copies in 2007 and returned as part of Metroid Prime: Trilogy in 2009.

main.title: Warhawk
main.subtitle: A battlefield shared between the ground and sky
main.summary: Warhawk is Incognito Entertainment's PlayStation 3 multiplayer action game, first released in North America on 28 August 2007. Soldiers, vehicles and aircraft fight over large maps, allowing the player to change roles within the same battle. A person defending an objective on foot can later take a vehicle or climb into a Warhawk to influence the fight from above. The different scales connect rather than occupy separate games. A threat in the sky matters to the people below, while a position captured on the ground can change what the surrounding battle allows.

cards.heading: A battlefield shared between the ground and sky
cards.text: Warhawk is Incognito Entertainment's PlayStation 3 multiplayer action game, first released in North America on 28 August 2007. Soldiers, vehicles and aircraft fight over large maps, allowing the player to change roles within the same battle. A person defending an objective on foot can later take a vehicle or climb into a Warhawk to influence the fight from above. The different scales connect rather than occupy separate games. A threat in the sky matters to the people below, while a position captured on the ground can change what the surrounding battle allows.

cards.heading: Choose the role the team needs now
cards.text: Deathmatch, team battles, Zones and Capture the Flag give the same maps different objectives. The player has to read both the immediate opposition and the larger situation: another aircraft may be a useful target, but a ground position can be more important to the result. Map configurations vary the space and conditions, encouraging different approaches to familiar terrain. Progress unlocks personnel and aircraft customisation, giving continued play another visible reward. The main attraction remains the ability to move between kinds of combat as the needs of the match change.

cards.heading: A PlayStation Network game with a physical edition
cards.text: Warhawk became the first PlayStation 3 release available both as a physical product and a PlayStation Network download. A planned single-player component was removed so development could concentrate on multiplayer. Dylan Jobe directed, with Christopher Lennertz and Timothy Michael Wynn composing the music. Updates addressed early technical issues and added further modes, while expansions supplied maps and equipment. Its later spiritual successor, Starhawk, continued the interest in a shared battlefield. Warhawk's original achievement was to make changing from a soldier to a pilot feel like a decision inside one continuing contest.

main.title: Heavenly Sword
main.subtitle: Nariko draws a powerful sword with a price attached
main.summary: Heavenly Sword is Ninja Theory's PlayStation 3 action adventure about Nariko, a warrior protecting her clan from King Bohan. The legendary sword she carries grants power at the cost of its wielder's life. Released in North America on 12 September 2007, the game follows her attempt to turn that dangerous inheritance against an approaching army.

cards.heading: A weapon that consumes its wielder
cards.text: Heavenly Sword is Ninja Theory's PlayStation 3 action adventure about Nariko, a warrior protecting her clan from King Bohan. The legendary sword she carries grants power at the cost of its wielder's life. Released in North America on 12 September 2007, the game follows her attempt to turn that dangerous inheritance against an approaching army.

cards.heading: Three stances, one encounter
cards.text: The sword's three stances answer different pressures. Speed uses two blades for quick exchanges, power joins them into a heavier weapon, and range extends the blades on chains to reach a wider group. Switching during an encounter changes how Nariko can interrupt an attack or create room to move. An enemy's approach therefore matters alongside the chosen combination: the useful response against one opponent may leave another free to close in.

cards.heading: Following the arrow
cards.text: Kai offers a different view of the conflict through her crossbow. Her sections ask the player to pick targets and guide shots with Aftertouch, following an arrow toward its destination. The same idea appears with projectiles elsewhere in the adventure. Steering a shot creates a small task inside the larger battle, with the camera holding attention on the space between weapon and target. The change of viewpoint gives a pause from Nariko's close-range combinations.

cards.heading: A performance inside the action
cards.text: The characters' performances were a major part of the production. Andy Serkis played Bohan and directed the actors, with performance capture connecting their movement and expressions to the scenes. Nariko's relationship with Kai and the enemy court's theatrical behaviour provide a tone beyond the combat. Nitin Sawhney's score accompanies that scale, moving between character moments and large confrontations as the story brings the cost of Nariko's weapon closer.
